by_task.when: Arizona law applies and the facts identify an item as medically or professionally prescribed assistive equipment for the debtor or a dependent.
by_task.procedure: Treat the item as a prescribed prosthetic or mobility aid under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(9) and claim its full value because the supplied provision states no dollar cap.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify prescribed assistive equipment as ordinary household furniture merely because it is used in the home; do not apply this rule to ordinary furniture lacking the prescription or assistive condition.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an asset fits a listed household-use category under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3), or is jewelry under § 522(d)(4).
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(3) for listed household furnishings, goods, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, and include § 522(d)(4) separately for jewelry. A value above the statutory cap limits the amount but does not defeat eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry under § 522(d)(3), omit an otherwise eligible item because its value exceeds a cap, or extend either provision to property outside its listed category.

by_task.when: An asset is considered under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) or is jewelry considered under § 522(d)(4).
by_task.procedure: First require that a § 522(d)(3) asset be one of the listed household-use categories, then assign no more than the lesser of its value and the $700 per-item limit. Evaluate jewelry separately under § 522(d)(4), using the lesser of value and $1,875 for one debtor. For jointly owned jewelry in a joint case, apply § 522(m) to each spouse's one-half interest and add the claims, each capped at $1,875.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $14,875 aggregate ceiling as the claim for one item, classify jewelry under § 522(d)(3), or double § 522(d)(3)'s $700 cap for a particular jointly owned item.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and the debtor or a dependent uses real or personal property as a residence.
by_task.procedure: Include 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(1) as an applicable residence alternative even when the residence's value exceeds $27,900.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $27,900 amount as an eligibility test or apply § 522(d)(1) to property that the facts do not identify as a residence, cooperative residence, or burial plot.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an estate asset is being evaluated.
by_task.procedure: For every asset, evaluate 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) as a separate alternative, including property also eligible under § 522(d)(1), another category-specific federal provision, or an allowable state provision.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit the wildcard because another exemption applies, because the asset exceeds the wildcard ceiling, or because a residence is listed; do not add it when the supplied allowable jurisdictions exclude federal exemptions.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an estate asset is being evaluated.
by_task.procedure: For 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5), calculate the independent claim as the lesser of the asset value and $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1). When no residence consumes that amount, use a $15,425 ceiling for one debtor. In a joint case, apply § 522(m) separately to each spouse's equal interest and add the two claims, so the combined ceiling is $30,850.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not aggregate allocations across assets, displace other applicable alternatives, assume unused homestead capacity when the facts show it has been consumed, or apply the two-debtor ceiling to a single debtor.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the debtor owns personal property.
by_task.procedure: Add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent alternative, including when a specific Illinois exemption also applies or the property's value exceeds $4,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat the $4,000 ceiling as an eligibility test, omit subsection (b) because subsection (a), (d), or (e) applies, or classify jewelry as necessary wearing apparel without facts establishing necessity.

by_task.when: Oregon law applies and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative even when the asset also fits a specific Oregon exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply it to real property or treat its $400 limit as a condition that makes a more valuable item ineligible.

by_task.when: Oregon law applies and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: For the independent Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) alternative, assign the lesser of the asset's value and $400.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not aggregate different assets or omit separately applicable Oregon exemptions.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania law applies to property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: For every property category, include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative alongside any specific Pennsylvania or federal exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not restrict § 8123 to cash, omit it because another exemption applies, or use its $300-per-spouse limit as an eligibility test for more valuable property.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania law applies to property of the judgment debtor.

by_task.avoid_when: Do not aggregate assets, replace a specific exemption, or exclude tangible property merely because the statute is titled a monetary exemption.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an estate asset is being evaluated.
by_task.procedure: Add an independent § 522(d)(5) claim. Unless the facts expressly say homestead capacity was consumed, use the lesser of value and $15,425 for one debtor. In a joint case, apply that ceiling to each spouse's one-half interest and add the results, producing the lesser of total value and $30,850.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not allocate the wildcard across assets, displace other alternatives, treat another exemption listed for the same asset as simultaneous consumption, or use the one-debtor ceiling for a joint case.

operations.rationale: Across current federal cases the parent continued omitting § 522(d)(5), and in the joint vehicle case used only the single-debtor ceiling. Targets consistently treat the wildcard as an independent alternative and apply the per-debtor ceiling to each equal interest.

by_task.when: Oregon law applies and the asset is personal property, including a vehicle, household good, wearing apparel, or trade tool.
by_task.procedure: Add Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative even when a specific Oregon exemption also applies and even when value exceeds $400.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply it to real property, omit it for business-use personal property, or treat the $400 limit as an eligibility condition.

by_task.when: Oregon law applies and the asset is personal property, including property also covered by a specific Oregon exemption.
by_task.procedure: Add an independent Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) claim equal to the lesser of the asset's value and $400.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not aggregate different assets, double the $400 claim merely because ownership is joint, or omit separately applicable Oregon exemptions.

operations.rationale: The parent repeatedly treated $400 as an eligibility cutoff or omitted subsection (p) when a vehicle, household, apparel, or trade exemption also applied. Current targets require this independent capped alternative.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania law applies to property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Add 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative for every property category, including property also covered by a federal or specific Pennsylvania exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not restrict § 8123 to cash, omit it because another exemption applies, or use its monetary limit as an eligibility test.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania law applies to property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: For § 8123, claim the lesser of value and $300 for one debtor. For jointly owned property of two spouses, apply $300 to each spouse's one-half interest and add the results, yielding the lesser of total value and $600.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not aggregate allocations across assets, replace another applicable exemption, use only $300 for qualifying joint property, or exclude tangible property because the provision is titled a monetary exemption.

operations.rationale: Current Pennsylvania cases omit § 8123, while the joint case also exposes the existing EV rule's incorrect single-spouse $300 amount. Seen targets use an independent alternative and combine two spouses' equal-interest claims up to $600.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the debtor owns personal property.
by_task.procedure: Add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent alternative, including when a specific Illinois exemption also applies or the property's value exceeds $4,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat the $4,000 ceiling as an eligibility test, omit subsection (b) because subsection (a), (d), or (e) applies, or classify jewelry as necessary wearing apparel without facts establishing necessity.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the debtor owns personal property.
by_task.procedure: Add a subsection (b) claim independently of any specific exemption. For one debtor, use the lesser of value and $4,000. For jointly owned property of two spouses, apply $4,000 to each spouse's one-half interest and add the results, yielding the lesser of total value and $8,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not output one aggregate exemption entry instead of asset-by-asset alternatives, omit subsection (b) for apparel or prescribed health aids, or infer a specific exemption such as health aid or trade tool without its factual condition.

operations.rationale: Current Illinois outputs omit subsection (b) for over-cap property and for apparel or health aids already covered specifically; the EV parent also failed to map claims by asset. The targets establish independent subsection (b) eligibility and spouse-by-spouse calculation.

by_task.when: Arizona law applies and the property is a musical instrument provided for the debtor's individual or family use.
by_task.procedure: Use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(2), treating its dollar amount as a claim limit rather than an eligibility test; for married debtors, § 33-1121 permits the spouses' exemptions to be combined in the instrument.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify a specifically prescribed musical instrument as ordinary household furnishings under § 33-1123, and do not apply this rule to nonmusical household property.

by_task.when: Arizona law applies and the property is a musical instrument provided for individual or family use.
by_task.procedure: Under § 33-1125(2), use the lesser of value and $400 for one debtor. For two spouses with equal interests, apply $400 to each half and add the claims, yielding the lesser of total value and $800.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not stop at $400 in a joint case, exceed $400 for a single debtor, or substitute § 33-1123 for the specifically listed instrument exemption.

operations.rationale: The parent misclassified the current musical instruments as household furnishings. The supplied statute specifically lists musical instruments, and the joint-debtor combination provision explains the released full-value claims above the single-spouse $400 limit.

by_task.when: Oregon law applies and personal-use property is a household good, furniture item, radio, television, or utensil.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(f) even when the property's value exceeds $3,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat $3,000 as an eligibility cutoff or extend subsection (f) to property lacking a household-use category or condition.

by_task.when: Oregon law applies and property satisfies a household-use category in Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(f).
by_task.procedure: Assign the lesser of the property's value and $3,000 under subsection (f), while retaining any independent subsection (p) alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not award the full value above $3,000, omit subsection (f) because value exceeds its cap, or replace subsection (p).

operations.rationale: The parent omitted Oregon's household exemption for current property valued just above its cap. The statute and targets show that the cap limits claim value rather than eligibility.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and the asset is one motor vehicle considered under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(2).
by_task.procedure: Assign the lesser of the vehicle's value and $4,450 for that vehicle, including when it is jointly owned.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not double the § 522(d)(2) amount for one jointly owned vehicle, omit an over-cap vehicle, or use this rule for more than one vehicle as a single claim.

operations.rationale: The current parent doubled the federal motor-vehicle cap for one jointly owned vehicle, while both seen joint-vehicle targets retain the $4,450 per-vehicle ceiling.
